utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it may be convenient if we refer to the Defence summary of affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I've done is prepared a document. I'm afraid it's not formally served, but it's a summary of our position. It follows the Defence list in order, and it sets out all that I have to say on the affidavits succinctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first five paragraphs explain our position, following on from the short discussion yesterday about the position the Defence will take, and I'll just read it out. There is material in all affidavits contrary to the Prosecution case. The Defence argument on the construction of Rule 94, now being taken on interlocutory appeal, is that objection to an affidavit makes it impossible for that affidavit to become part of the evidence in the trial. The Trial Chamber takes a different view --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Inaudible] ... the Prosecution agrees -- I'm so sorry -- pending resolution of the interlocutory appeal, that it is the Chamber which decides whether an affidavit should be read following any objection. Your Honour, I omitted to get copies of this for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm trying to get them produced now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you could then speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has the power to order an affidavit witness to be called for cross-examination of its own motion, i.e., even if there is no objection. In these circumstances, the Prosecution formally objects to all affidavits, simply to ensure its position is preserved and overall fairness obtained if -- in the event the Defence interpretation of Rule 94 is found by the Appeals Chamber to be correct. And the Chamber will recall that the Defence has objected to the adduction of any and every affidavit in the Prosecution's case. To assist the Chamber, the Prosecution sets out particular reasons, in relation to certain witnesses, why the witness should be called for cross-examination. And then dealing with them in order, and I shan't read all matters out, for some of them are matters better not read out but the Chamber can read them, but so far as Tokic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Before going to the examination of each affidavit, personally I cannot agree with your interpretation of the position of the Defence and what is going on now in the appeal, what is at stake in the interlocutory appeal. [Interpretation] I believe that we cannot move ahead in this way. We all know, here in this Chamber, why there has been an appeal and what the motivations for it were. We all are aware of the circumstances in which your affidavits came in and were accepted, with a specific interpretation provided by the Chamber. Therefore, starting from what you just said, namely, that what is at stake at the appeals level is that an objection to an affidavit is such that it is no longer possible for the affidavit to become an exhibit before the Chamber. Starting from that cannot be done. The problem doesn't lie there. The problem raised by the Defence is the interpretation to be given to 94 ter as provided by the Defence and also heard by the Chamber. It is not true that any objection makes it impossible to maintain the affidavit. Can you start from such an interpretation that you will systematically make an objection to affidavits in order to reserve your position? I don't think that is an acceptable point of view. Now, as we said, and this was decided upon yesterday, you have to provide your rationale and your motivation affidavit by affidavit. There is no general stance on absences as to affidavits. That has been decided upon yesterday. We shall not come back on this. We shall make a decision affidavit by affidavit, either that, we retain your objection, or we turn it down. So this is where we are at today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've read the Defence motion in the Appeal Chamber. They are seeking a ruling to the effect that if there is an objection, an affidavit cannot be allowed in evidence. It's not an interpretation with which I agree, but inevitably in this Tribunal, if that's what the Appeal Chamber decides, that will be, for the time being, the law of the Chamber. What I have done is, I hope respectful of the potential for precedent authority to be effective in this Tribunal but nevertheless entirely constructive and helpful to the Chamber, I stand by my position and dealing, as the Chamber wanted, witness by witness, with whether there are particular reasons, in addition to the general objection which I state for the purposes set out in this short document. For Tokic, there are no particular reasons. However, we observe that the man is a commander who might be expected to have direct knowledge of matters in issue, and there may be a pattern emerging of the Defence seeking to rely by affidavit on such senior members of the HVO, witnesses who would find it less easy to assert ignorance of events, as have many of the witnesses so far called have. I turn then to Ivica Drmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you wait a little, because we want to make a decision on each case. [Trial Chamber deliberates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There being no particular ground of objection beyond what is set out in the paper, this affidavit is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that the next three should be considered together for they all cover the Donja Veceriska bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cover the bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remind us, this is the Midhat Haskic incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The admissibility of his statement being subject to another appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, there was the evidence of Mr. -- I mean the statement of Mr. Haskic on the point for the Prosecution, and the Defence have called -- I will be reminded of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They have called Branko Drmic and Mile Vinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So they have called two witnesses and these are two other witnesses on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to take the -- consider these two together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ivica Drmic claims to have been in a bar but that was not supported by Branko who did not recall his presence and that's a particular feature in respect of both of them, the incident generally the Chamber might think which warrants all eyewitnesses being called because of its potential significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I hope it's apparent to the Trial Chamber that we've employed a method in our approach to the presentation of evidence, it's topic by topic, and we see no reason to bring four witnesses to testify about a topic when one or two are sufficient. We believe that the one or two that we have produced are sufficient. Producing two more would simply lengthen proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Did you present one or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two, Branko Drmic and Mile Vinac, but the reason we did so, Your Honour, was because they actually testified to two different kinds of points. Their testimony did not overlap completely. If it had, we would only have produced one witness. As we understand it, the whole purpose of Rule 94 ter is to expedite proceedings by producing purely corroborative affidavits, and that's exactly what we did. These affidavits corroborate the testimony of the live witnesses. They don't adduce any additional evidence beyond what has already been testified about and our position is calling either or both of these gentlemen would merely be duplicative of the evidence that's already been adduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered the submissions in relation to this incident in the bar and we think the matter is sufficiently covered by the evidence we've heard. Of course by doing so, we make no indication at all as to any ruling, any finding, rather, of fact, which we may make but as far as the evidence is concerned, we don't think it's a matter which the objection or the requirement for cross-examination can be sustained having regard to the totality of the evidence and its importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next three Arapovic, Kristo and Santic all deal with the checkpoint incident. And again, the proposition is advanced that this is an incident sufficiently important for all eyewitnesses to be called. I don't read out publicly what's item two against Milenko Arapovic, nor item two in relation to Kristo, nor item two in relation to Santic. They are matters that the Chamber may want to have in mind when it considers whether these are witnesses who can properly be taken by way of affidavit in this important piece of the case, or important piece of evidence which is a discreet incident within the case and which, of course, is the only part of the case, I suppose, which is close in general feel and substance to an ordinary straightforward criminal allegation and trial. So those are the points we make about those three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of points I'd like to make on that. First of all, it can't have escaped the Trial Chamber's attention that this particular incident is not charged anywhere in the indictment. It certainly hasn't escaped our attention. A point has been made that some sort of an alibi defence should have been asserted by the -- by the Defence, but as I've informed the Prosecution, it's not our policy to assert alibi defences to charges which are not specifically made in the amended indictment. That's the first point that I wanted to make. The second point that I wanted to make is the two witnesses that we have produced on this incident as the Trial Chamber will remember were Josip Grubicic and Ivo Arar. We produced them for different reasons. Ivo Arar was the actual escort in the car containing Mr. Kostroman that was actually stopped at the checkpoint. Mr. Grubicic was one of a group of people that travelled down to the checkpoint to assist Mr. Kostroman having -- Mr. Bogdan Santic having received a call from Mr. Kostroman's car over a walkie-talkie. These three witnesses corroborate the testimony of both of the live witnesses that we have testified. For the reasons that I have previously articulated, we do not think that it's necessary to bring five witnesses when two cover the point sufficiently, although they don't cover the same factual points in precise detail, they did overlap on one significant point and that is the fact that Mr. Kordic was not there, and these affidavits all corroborate that. We see no reason why these people should be brought before the Court to give evidence which is essentially completely duplicative of that that has been given by two witnesses. And actually, as my colleague points out, some of the Busovaca witnesses that we will be producing next week and the week after that are going to give evidence broadly consistent with the information contained in these affidavits as well as the testimony in court of Mr. Grubicic and Mr. Arar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Sayers, is it about the -- this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: The witnesses who are to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: About the Kacuni checkpoint incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Their testimony is going to cover a lot more territory than this. I mean we have produced the Kacuni witnesses that we had intended to call and had planned to call in our presentation of our case. But other witnesses in our case covering many other topics will also give what knowledge they have of who was involved in the Kacuni checkpoint incident. Of course the only issue, I think, that is relevant to this entire incident is the single question of was Mr. Kordic there, and we think the evidence is pretty clear that he was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Even if we decide, and we haven't, we've got to consider it, but I want to make it plain at the outset of this discussion about affidavits. You assert that you think you've brought sufficient evidence. Well that's a matter for you, of course, and your submission on the topic. The fact that if we do rule that cross-examination is not necessary does not mean that we accept that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I fully understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we shall have to make our judgement at the end, and our findings on the evidence which is laid before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want you to be under any misunderstanding, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would you help us to this extent: Of these three, I seem to remember that Arapovic's name was mentioned. Can you help us with the evidence on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't help you immediately, but I can swiftly find it. Yes. Witness T said that when they were stopped by the soldiers at the lower point, that the -- this is in relation to other matters. Arapovic was mentioned as a person who detained Witness T at the fish ponds. That may be one of the reasons you're remembering that unusual name. And he gave a graphic account of how they were then detained and dealt with. That's one of his appearances in the evidence. I'll see where the next ones are. I think that's probably -- that's the reference outside this area that he's been referred to, so he features -- I perhaps should have dealt with that there -- he features independently in the evidence, it would appear, as somebody showing partiality and doing bad things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you assist us as to this: Were either of the other two, Kristo or Bogdan Santic, mentioned in relation to the Kacuni incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Other than by Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Other than by Defence witnesses. By the Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just check on that. I think "probably not" is the way it's looking at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, having regard to the issues raised -- this is an important incident -- we have to balance the need for cross-examination of witnesses with the need for expedition, and we have come to the conclusion that Milenko Arapovic should be called for cross-examination. In relation to the other two, their affidavits will be admitted on the basis which I've already explained, that it doesn't mean that there is any finding in relation to this incident, as that's what we'll have to do. But we're prepared to admit those affidavits. But in the case of Mr. Arapovic, because he has been mentioned in the Prosecution evidence, we think it right that the Prosecution should be able to cross-examine him. Yes. Now, going on, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Len Santic. No particular reason, but he's -- I set out what's known about his background and about one or two of the contacts which I think will be familiar names in light of the Ahmici incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit that affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mario Santic, he touches the Breljas evidence, which is obviously of potential importance. He's former Vitezovi and HOS, and you can see what's said in number 3. The Chamber may think that it may be inappropriate to allow reliance without seeing this witness on what he would be saying about that critical incident at a critical point of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. To remind ourselves, this is Mr. Breljas' evidence that Mr. Kordic was at the Dubravica barracks at a meeting on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 15th, but it's fair to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Query --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Query 15th or 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 15th or 16th, and therefore no doubt the Prosecution would rely on that evidence as showing a connection between the accused and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And this witness contradicts that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, anything you want to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. As you can see in the summary of Mr. Santic's evidence that we've filed, he was actually wounded in Mlakici on April the 17th, 1993. The testimony that he provides is almost completely duplicative of what Mr. Buha testified about. But if the Trial Chamber wants him here, obviously he'll come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, yes, we do. We think he should be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness, Ljuba Vidovic, as you can see from the summary provided in the Defence document, deals with what she saw on television on particular occasions in considerable detail. Such a witness would probably not, in the overall setting of this case, require or justify any particular reason to be called, but we can't help but note that the degree of recollection that she claims is maybe itself improbable and is in contrast to the evidence she gave in Kupreskic to the effect that she had no interest in politics and had a poor memory. I observe that it might be sufficient for this particular problem to be resolved, if her affidavit is to be read, by the relevant transcript in Kupreskic also being taken into account as being another account of her interest in politics and the state of her memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to comment on that, Your Honour, because we've just received the document that has been distributed today, and I do not have in mind the Kupreskic testimony that Ms. Vidovic gave. Her testimony seems to be fairly basic, and that is, that she has no recollection whatsoever of any of the kinds of comments attributed to Mr. Kordic on two separate occasions ever having been made, and there is plenty of other evidence to the same effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit the affidavit. If there is a submission in relation to the transcript, we'll consider that at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mario Mlakic, who worked at TV Vitez, no particular reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevin Maric, there is one additional fact that I ought to have drawn to your attention beyond what's on the little schedule, and that is that his name is not on the Defence witness list. So far as he is concerned, he is a former commander of the brigade in Kakanj, and he sets out quite detailed evidence. I note that he sets out, somewhat elliptically, his contacts with and the visits by the defendant Dario Kordic. He says he met him during the war, that Mr. Kordic did not visit Kakanj after September of 1992 and was never in Vares at any time in 1993. So the picture of contacts is far from clear. And this is a commander, a person in a senior position, but it's Kakanj. So there are reasons why the Chamber might prefer to see this person to have these matters clarified. And in any event, he was not a listed witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pavo Barac, no particular reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last witness, one for whom there are several reason why he should be called, Novi Travnik is his area. And Novi Travnik, of course, unlike some of the other locations, features in several of the accounts in the indictment. As president of the HDZ, he's an important political figure who should be able to give first-hand evidence of political influence in Novi Travnik in the war. His denial of contact with Kordic should be explored in cross-examination, and he should know more, it may be, than the witness recently called yesterday. The circumstances of his appointment to his position would need to be explored. He was thought to be with Kordic in Novi Travnik in February, discussing the Bratstvo factory matter. To be explored. In March, he appeared with Kordic on the television, discussing military and arms issues, and of course he should be the person or a person able to deal with and confirm or, alternatively, not able to confirm the 21st of January, 1993 meeting which relates on to the checkpoint incident and, indeed, on which some of the checkpoint defence is built. So in our respectful submission, this would be a witness of potential value, and it would not be appropriate, in our submission, for his evidence to come in by affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, when we decide which witnesses to bring before the Court, we have to make informed decisions relating to the issues that are specifically raised by the Prosecution's evidence. In Novi Travnik, we think we've produced two witnesses who address the general allegations about Novi Travnik in a fairly specific way. Mr. Sekic's affidavit confirms Mr. Civcija's testimony again in a general way. His affidavit doesn't cover any specific factual issues. It just generally corroborates the picture of events over a one-and-a-half-year period that Mr. Civcija gave to the Court yesterday and the day before. There's no mention of the checkpoint incident in this affidavit, and that would be beyond the scope of direct examination anyway. Once again, I guess if the Court thinks that it's necessary to bring yet another Novi Travnik witness to testify, we can do that. But the only concern that I have is this: We've given a good-faith estimate to be finished our case by the August break, and I'm happy to inform the Court that we are on schedule to do that and we're going to make our committed efforts to continue to do that. Obviously, we have some significant witnesses coming up and we'll have to re-evaluate the position. But I have plotted out our case for the 12-week period, and we're at the end of week 4, one third of the way through our case, and we're exactly where we thought we would be. If witnesses are called and subjected to extensive cross-examination of the type that we've seen so far, that may jeopardise the schedule and require us to compress other evidence. If it does, we'll obviously try to continue to adhere to our deadline, but we don't think that it's necessary to bring a person like this to the court to give more general testimony of the kind that drew comment from the Court when it was being gone over by my colleague Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've considered this with care. The affidavit is in very general terms following and corroborating evidence which has already been given. The grounds for wanting to cross-examine a witness in this case or really, that more information could be obtained from him, the Prosecution hoped, and given the various factors that we have to take into account, we don't think that's sufficient to order his presence here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Items six and seven, can I just turn to the third page. At the moment, the Defence witness list being served covers two weeks at most and, typically, we try to give six weeks or the whole run of our witnesses projected to the Defence when we could. We've just seen one affidavit which comes from somebody not on the list at all, which the Chamber has allowed in but in any event, the Defence witness list, that is the list of witnesses forthcoming does not include affidavit witnesses who are to be served and so far, they've all or nearly all been served immediately before the witness being corroborated is called. The seven days allowed in the rules, as a matter of fact, is not sufficient for us. It's insufficient for us to conduct the sort of inquiries into affidavit witnesses and their backgrounds to give you the best assistance we can -- we should be able to give you. There's no complaint in that. I'm just saying that that's simply the difficulty we face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, if, in a particular case, it's a difficulty, if it's a general witness, I don't anticipate that there would be much difficulty in a week. But if there is, say in the case of the last witness, that there is a broad area which you wish to look at, then it's open to you to make an application for an extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the other area is the sort of matter that you've seen referred to in, for example, Mr. Arapovic and item two on us that might be available to us in seven days or that might be information of background that only comes outside that period of time. So I draw it to your attention. What we would be assisted by, and it would seem to us that this should really be the position, is being notified in advance of what affidavit witnesses are going to be tendered so that we can start the process of making our inquiries as the same time that we are in a position to making our inquiries in respect of the witnesses they support. It would seem to us that is consistent with the general policy of being given an advanced list or a list of witnesses advance of them coming to give evidence one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, can you assist as to that? We note that you are on target and commend the way in which you have been conducting the matter. But there is a problem about the future which is this: That at the moment, a large number of names have been given and it's impossible for the Court or anybody else to know which of those, in fact, are coming or likely to give affidavits. And that may, in turn, cause delays by the other side having to ask for time to make inquiries. Now, can we at some stage have a list, a firm list, or as firm as possible list of those who you hope to call, those whom you hope to call by way of affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Aspirationally, I would be delighted to do that, Your Honour, and I think that we can, if it would be helpful to the Prosecution, we can give a list of the affidavits witnesses that we intend -- or the affidavits that we intend to try to acquire each two week period. In other words, when we give a two week batting order, as we've been asked to do by the Trial Court, and which we've done, we could also alert the Prosecution as to the affidavits that we are going to try to collect, if we can, and indicate which particular witnesses those affidavits are going to corroborate. If that would be helpful. But I can say right now, we -- it's always difficult to come up with a precise number of the total number of witnesses that we intend to call, but I think it's about 60, and I would note that we have called 20 to date, and we're one-third of the way through so that sounds right. And I also would like to alert the court, if I may, we may as well do it right now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one thing. For the next two weeks, are you in a position to give the names of the affidavit witnesses? You needn't give them now, but can you pass them to the Prosecution today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We can pass to the Prosecution today the ones that we are reasonably sure that we can get, and maybe indicate the ones that we would hope to get if we could. I'd prefer not to do the latter, because that might expose the affiant to unnecessary attention, but we can certainly alert the Prosecution that we are fairly certain of the ones we can get and I can do that today. Yes, Your Honour. And with respect to Mr. Arapovic and Mr. Santic, we would propose if we can persuade these gentlemen to come in to testify the week after next, so we can stay on our projected schedule. Their testimony should be relatively short, I trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's one other matter that I would like to raise, Your Honour, and it may sound trivial, it probably is trivial, but it's a matter of judicial notice the about the death of Dr. Ante Starcevic. We've previously provided the Prosecution with an extract from a book which states that Dr. Ante Starcevic died in 1895. It seems to be an incontrovertable and simple, historical fact that would be appropriate for the Court -- of which the Court should take judicial notice and I can distribute to the Court, if it's necessary, the extract of the book upon which contains this historical fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you it in translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So why don't you hand it in? Who was he, at a matter of interest?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was a prominent Croatian or a prominent Croatian politician who died in 1895 had no relationship whatsoever to do with the Ustasa, as indicated. And I've highlighted the passage upon which we rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other matters; one very short. We've been provided with the names of two witnesses, confidential witnesses, but no summaries yet and, no doubt, that's oversight. But the summaries should presumably be served in accordance with the Court's general order about summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do not recall any order requiring summaries, but if the Prosecution wants a summary of the expected testimony of those witnesses, we will provide it to them this weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point, can I revert to the tape, to make things one step apparently more complicated, but in the second step rather more -- rather more encouraging, rather better. The end position may be when we look at things, and I'm not sure about this, but the end position may be that in fact the Registry has had the original tape all along. Now I must explain why that's a possibility and what has to be done. The -- it's something that's only come to light this morning. First of all, it is necessary to go back and remember the detail about what happened. I'm sorry about this, but it's an unusual event and it's got to be recalled from memory. What happened was, as the Chamber will recall, that the witness produced it in the witness box, although it wasn't this courtroom. It went straight from the witness to what would be the equivalent of the room behind me now for playing, and while it was in that room, it was copied. The session ended, the witness left, and the Audio-Visual Department distributed the tape provided and the copies. The invariable practice in the institution in respect of tapes has been that the original is retained in the evidence unit and copies are provided for playing and so on. That practice was undoubtedly reflected in the understanding of the Registrar that what they had was a copy because that's what they always get, and it was reflected in the understanding of the OTP that the document thereafter logged and dealt with in the evidence unit was the original produced by the witness. And it may still be the case that that's exactly what happened. But remember, it all happened so quickly. The witness produced it, and it went straight in to be played, I think, that it never really touched our hands. Yesterday afternoon, pursuant to the order, the tape, whatever it was, was taken by Ms. Greenwood and Ms. Verhaag to the Registry for handing over and for signing off on the chain of custody record. Ms. Verhaag noticed that the retained version in the Registry, that is, what was thought to be the Registry copy, which she also saw last week, looked older than the version we had and that was taken down there. Also it's a different make of tape. That's not surprising. Inquiries have been made in a neutral way of the witness as to what make of tape he believes he had, the copy. And his account matches the make of tape held in the Registry, the one he handed over. It will be helpful to know from the Defence, when they have had had a chance to look at their document, what the make of tape is they have. Because although it may be that the Audio-Visual Unit uses different tapes and different makes of tapes from time to time, it may be that if their make of tape is the same as the one that we have and thought to be the original, that, in fact, the original has always been in the Registry, and that what we all have were copies. And that the understanding or misunderstanding derived from what's the normal practice in this court. So I would be grateful if, at some stage, the Defence could let us know what make of -- I don't imagine they know now, what make of tape theirs is and for the time being, both the document, the tape that the Registry originally had on the day and the version that was provided yesterday will, of course, stay with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we will order a written report on all this for both tapes, covering both tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we'll get to the bottom of it. Perhaps the Defence would help with the make of their tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We would. We've got a digital audiotape that's been given to us by the Prosecution -- by the Registry. I can't remember what the make of that is, and the other tape, if we have one, I've never even seen it so I don't know what the make is, but we'll certainly make inquiries and report to the Court. It might help if the Prosecution could provide the Court as an attachment to its report the chain of custody records for this -- for these tapes because I can say for myself, the position is completely confused. I can't follow which -- what what's the original, what's the copy, whose had them and where they've been or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report is being prepared now, and all that can be dealt with and will be dealt with swiftly, but if the Defence, who were provided the same day by the Audio-Visual Department the tape, the make of the tape, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there are any other matters, we will adjourn until Monday morning at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
